## Language Understanding

Search engines work best when customers use the exact words that appear in product titles. When they don't — whether they use a synonym, a descriptive phrase, or a conversational question — the engine needs to bridge that gap. For Huckberry, this is the single most damaging capability failure: customers describing what they want in plain language are consistently walking away empty-handed, even when the store stocks exactly what they're looking for.

**"something to keep my food cold on a camping trip"**
The search returned nothing at all — even though the store carries coolers and insulated food storage products like the YETI Tundra and Osprey x Hydro Flask Campcore Carryout Cooler. The engine could not connect the phrase "keep my food cold" to any product because none of those words appear in a product title.

**"warm jacket for hiking in cold weather"**
The search returned nothing at all — even though the store carries an entire jackets category. Words like "warm," "hiking," and "cold weather" are descriptions of what a jacket does, not what it's called, and the engine has no way to make that connection.

**"what should i bring to a backyard barbecue"**
The search returned nothing at all — even though the store carries grilling tools, fire pit accessories, outdoor tableware, and coolers that directly answer this question. The engine saw no product titled "what should i bring to a backyard barbecue" and gave up.

**"shoes i can wear hiking but also around town"**
The search returned nothing at all — even though the store carries trail runners, hiking sneakers, and hybrid boots built precisely for this dual-purpose use. The engine cannot interpret a use-case description; it can only match words.

**"cooler bag"**
Here results did appear, but the best one was buried. The Rugged Road Tardigrade Backpack Cooler — which has "cooler" directly in its title and scored significantly higher than everything else — was pushed to positions #4 and #5, while three slots of the YETI Camino Carryall Totes (general-purpose totes, not coolers) occupied the top three spots.

Customer saw:
- #1–3: YETI Camino Carryall 50L / 35L Tote

Should have seen:
- #1–2: Rugged Road Tardigrade Backpack Cooler
- #3: YETI Camino Carryall 35L Tote

## Prioritized Roadmap

1. **Add a product-type and intent boost layer so the right kind of product ranks first**
When a query names a product type — "jacket," "pizza oven," "boots," "tote" — that word should act as a strong filter, ensuring items in the matching category rank above accessories, apparel, or unrelated products that merely share a brand name. This fixes the core ranking disorder across Brand & Model Search (Arc'teryx Conveyor Belt ranking above the Arc'teryx Gamma Jacket for "Arc jacket"), Typo Tolerance (Patagonia Nano Puff Mitts ranking above jackets for "Patgonia jacket" and "Patagonia jackets"), Product Discovery (Gozney Dome XL Stand ranking above the Osprey Campcore Cooking Tool Roll & Utensil Set for "outdoor kitchen tools"), and the Rugged Road Tardigrade Backpack Cooler being buried below YETI Carryall Totes for "cooler bag."
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

2. **Build a semantic / intent search layer to handle descriptive and conversational queries**
The engine currently returns zero results for any query that describes what a product does rather than naming it — "something to keep my food cold on a camping trip," "warm jacket for hiking in cold weather," "something to sit on while camping," "something to cook pizza outdoors," "gear to carry all my camping stuff," and "keep drinks cold at the beach" all returned nothing or irrelevant clothing. Deploying a semantic retrieval layer (using text embeddings or a similar approach) would map these descriptions to the right product categories, fixing the most widespread and severe failures across Language Understanding, Shopping Context, and Filters & Constraints.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Major Project

3. **Map occasion, gift, and seasonal queries to the relevant category pages**
Queries like "birthday present for an outdoorsy guy," "gift for dad who loves grilling," "summer grilling gifts," "holiday gifts for hikers," "housewarming gift for someone who cooks outside," and "camping trip essentials for a weekend away" all returned zero results despite the store carrying directly relevant inventory. The site already has merchandised categories — Grilling & Fire Pits, Outdoor Equipment, Jackets — that answer these queries. Connecting occasion and gift-intent phrasing to those existing category pages (via synonym rules, intent mapping, or curated redirects) would immediately stop the bleed on high-value seasonal and gifting traffic.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

4. **Implement negation parsing so "not [attribute]" queries exclude the right products**
The engine currently ignores the word "not" entirely. For "hat not wool," every result contained wool — including the Huckberry Boiled Wool Striped Beanie at #1. For "boots not waterproof," the Salomon XT-6 GTX Trail Sneaker (Gore-Tex, explicitly waterproof) occupied the top three positions. For "cooler not soft-sided," the search returned nothing rather than surfacing hard-sided coolers like the YETI Tundra. Parsing "not [term]" and "without [term]" as exclusion signals — and mapping those signals to the relevant product attributes and tags — fixes all three Filters & Constraints negation failures.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

5. **Deduplicate variant cards so each product appears once and more of the assortment is visible**
Across nearly every capability tested, the same product fills multiple result slots as separate size or color variant cards: the Huckberry Japanese Rib Knit Beanie appeared five times for "beanie," the Relwen Micropile Half-Zip appeared three times for "fleece pullover," the L.L.Bean Boat & Tote appeared six times for "canvas tote bag," and the Fjallraven Vidda Pro Lite Shorts appeared four times for the partial query "Fjall." Collapsing variants into a single result card — with size and color selectable on the product page — would free up the displaced slots and surface buried higher-relevance products like the Florence Marine X Polartec Alpha Direct Hooded Fleece and the Steele Canvas Everyday Canvas Tote.
Impact: Moderate | Effort: Medium Effort

6. **Apply a minimum relevance threshold and category guard to prevent off-topic padding**
Several queries returned results that had no business appearing: swim shorts and sunglasses for "travel bag," body oil and honey for the partial query "Heli," and a beach shirt repeated five times for "keep drinks cold at the beach." Setting a minimum relevance floor (so low-scoring results are suppressed rather than shown) and a category guard (so a boots query cannot return hats, and a bag query cannot return swimwear) would clean up these pages. When a partial query like "Heli" genuinely matches only two products, the engine should return two results honestly rather than padding to fifteen with unrelated items.
Impact: Moderate | Effort: Quick Win

7. **Handle catalog gaps gracefully by honoring the product-type noun over the brand name**
When a brand-plus-product-type query has no matching inventory — as with "Fjallraven backpack," where no Fjallraven backpack exists — the engine currently drops the product type entirely and floods the page with brand apparel variants. The better behavior is either to return backpacks from other brands (honoring what the customer actually asked for) or to show a clear no-results message with a suggestion. This also covers the "HF water bottle" case, where an uncommon abbreviation returned nothing; a "did you mean Hydro Flask?" prompt would recover the session.
Impact: Minor | Effort: Quick Win

This audit was conducted using our search-quality audit pipeline — a seven-phase automated search quality assessment. 60 test queries were generated across 15 query categories, grouped into 6 core capabilities.

**1. Site Discovery**
Automated analysis of your site's structure, navigation categories, brands, and featured products to understand what your search engine should be able to find.

Site-type-aware selection from a library of 26 test categories. Categories are chosen based on your site's commerce model to ensure the audit tests what matters most for your customers.

**3. Query Generation**
AI-generated realistic customer queries grounded in the actual products, brands, and categories found on your site — not generic templates.

**4. Result Collection**
Automated search execution collecting the top results for each test query exactly as your customers would see them.

**5. Relevance Scoring**
Each result scored on a 0.0–1.0 scale by a specialized relevance model, producing an objective measure of how well each result matches the query intent.

**6. Failure Analysis**
Each query classified by failure mode (e.g., no results, category not understood, constraint ignored, typo not handled, or relevant results buried) and assigned a severity based on customer impact — whether the search returned nothing, surfaced the wrong products, or simply ordered the right ones poorly.

Findings synthesized into this actionable narrative with prioritized recommendations ordered by business impact.
